facts.text: Design of experiments (DOE) is strongest when the objective is to estimate which factors and interactions materially affect detection distance, stopping margin or false alarms.

facts.text: Fractional factorial designs sharply reduce the number of experimental runs but intentionally alias higher-order effects.

facts.text: Response-surface designs characterise curvature in a smaller influential subspace after influential factors have been identified.

facts.text: D-optimal designs are useful when constraints make standard factorial grids impossible, but sacrifice orthogonality.
facts.quote: D-optimal designs are useful when constraints make standard factorial grids impossible, at the cost of orthogonality.

facts.text: The NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods documents fractional factorial, screening, response-surface and D-optimal designs.

facts.text: Design of experiments can support claims about main effects and low-order interactions of parameters on a continuous response, such as detection range against dust density and illumination.

facts.text: Design of experiments can provide good space-filling coverage for training surrogate models.

facts.text: Design of experiments cannot establish failure probability in the field because its design points are not weighted by real-world frequency.

facts.text: Design of experiments cannot claim detection of narrow failure regions between design points.
facts.quote: Cannot claim: failure probability in the field, because the design points are not weighted by real-world frequency; detection of narrow failure regions between design points.

facts.text: The validity of design-of-experiments conclusions depends on the response model and alias assumptions.

facts.text: Space-filling schemes, including Latin hypercube, Sobol and other quasi-random designs, distribute virtual experiments across continuous parameters more evenly than naive random draws.
